title: The Simpsons Season 38: Emma Thompson, Chimps, and a $200 Cup
summary:
The Simpsons is back for its 38th season, and the premiere is a love letter to children's books — with a twist.

Airing September 27, 2026, "The Children's Book Job" features Emma Thompson as Constance Clavinger, a beloved children's author who arrives in Springfield for a benefit to save the elementary school. But Clavinger is no gentle librarian. She gets drunk at the airport bar, and Homer is tasked with getting her to a school book fair organized by Marge. Think of it like the movie Get Him to the Greek — but with Homer Simpson.

"If you're going to write a giant guest part, you want an icon, a bucket list person like Emma Thompson," executive producer Matt Selman told Variety. "She threw herself into it with full gusto."

The episode also features Colin Jost as himself, reading his own children's book to a thoroughly unimpressed audience. In one daydream sequence, Springfield transforms into worlds from The Very Hungry Caterpillar, Richard Scarry's books, Captain Underpants, and Diary of a Wimpy Kid. Selman calls it a tribute to "generational children's artists."

More episodes are on the way. "Diary of a Chimpy Kid" (Oct. 4) follows Bart and Lisa as they adopt a baby chimp — and Homer panics after watching a YouTube video about adult chimps. "Testing 1-2-3" explores neurodiversity. And "Treehouse of Horror XXXVII" (Oct. 25) opens with a Nightmare Before Christmas mashup, then features a segment where Homer emerges from the shed as a different husband for Marge — suddenly she's married to Lenny, or Kang and Kodos. Tiffany Haddish guest-stars as Marge's sassy best friend.

The show has also teamed up with Jack in the Box for a "Munchie Meal of Horror" with six glow-in-the-dark collectible cups. They sold out immediately and are now reselling on eBay for $200. Selman jokes that he warned the company to make enough cups. "And guess what? They didn't!"

The cups are packed with Easter eggs, including a callback to Bart's twin brother Hugo from Season 8 — now eating a Jack in the Box fish sandwich. "It's just very fun to do a 30-year fish callback," Selman says.
why_it_matters: A show running for 38 seasons is a case study in how a single franchise can shape generations of viewers, spin off a merchandise economy and keep reworking other people's childhoods — here, children's books — into its own jokes. It also shows how tightly television, streaming clips and retail collectibles are now tied together.

background_read: The Simpsons (an American animated sitcom created by Matt Groening) first aired in 1989 and is the longest-running scripted primetime series in U.S. television history — which is the only reason a 38th season is even possible.

Its annual 'Treehouse of Horror' Halloween special has been a tradition since the early 1990s and regularly borrows characters like the aliens Kang and Kodos (the show's recurring extraterrestrial villains) for its parodies.

Emma Thompson (a British actress equally known for serious dramas and comedy) is exactly the kind of guest the show books for a large role, while Colin Jost (a writer and 'Weekend Update' co-anchor on Saturday Night Live) appears as himself.

The episode's daydream sequence draws on books many viewers grew up with, from The Very Hungry Caterpillar to Diary of a Wimpy Kid (a hugely popular illustrated series about a middle-schooler), turning nostalgia into animation.

Fast-food tie-ins are a long-running Simpsons pattern; Jack in the Box (a U.S. fast-food chain) is just the latest partner, and the glow-in-the-dark cups selling out and then resurfacing on eBay at high prices shows how merchandise becomes a collector market.

perspectives.description: Fans get a star guest, a nostalgia-packed daydream sequence and collectible merchandise that makes the season feel like an event, while Jack in the Box gets millions of dollars of free attention from a sell-out. Emma Thompson's casting also signals that the show can still attract serious actors.

Long-running shows lean heavily on guest stars, callbacks and brand partnerships, which critics see as substitutes for new ideas. A merchandise tie-in that sells out and then reappears online at many times its original price also raises questions about who actually gets to enjoy the promotion.

Branded fast-food tie-ins and limited-edition collectibles have been part of American television marketing for decades, and secondary resale markets routinely form around them. For a series this old, merchandise and nostalgia are not extras — they are part of how the show stays financially viable.

The season will test whether a 38th run can still find new subjects, with episodes on chimpanzees and neurodiversity suggesting the writers are reaching for fresher ground. How those episodes are received — particularly around neurodiversity — may matter more to the show's legacy than any cup.
